transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you—please have a seat. What brings you in today, and what would you like help with right now?

I’m constantly forgetting little everyday things—appointments, errands, even finishing what I start for the community center. It’s starting to cause problems with the people I work with there and at home, and I’d like to understand why this is happening and what I can do about it.

When you’re trying to remember or finish things, do you mainly feel restless and worried, or more sad, low on energy, and uninterested, or is it more like your mind just jumps around and you can’t hold your focus even when you try?

It feels more like my mind just jumps around and I can’t hold my focus, even when I’m really trying to. I’ll start something with good intentions, then get pulled off by other thoughts or distractions and only later realize I never finished what I meant to do.

Aside from the focus problems, do you often feel physically tense or on edge and worry a lot about many different things, or do you more often feel down, lose interest in things you used to enjoy, and have low energy most days?

I wouldn’t say I’m especially down or losing interest—I still enjoy my activities and usually have decent energy. I do worry some, mostly about letting people down or forgetting something important, but I wouldn’t call it constant or overwhelming tension.

Have these concentration and forgetfulness problems been present in some form since you were a child or teenager, or do you feel they started more clearly later in adult life after an illness, injury, or major stressor?

Looking back, I think they’ve been there since I was a kid—teachers used to say I was bright but daydreamed, rushed, and talked out of turn, and my mom was always after me for not finishing chores. They’ve just become much more noticeable and disruptive in the last couple of years since I’ve been more fully retired and took on more planning at the community center.
Have you ever had a significant head injury, stroke, seizure, or serious brain infection at any point in your life, and if so did your attention or memory get noticeably worse after that event?
I’ve never had a serious head injury, stroke, seizure, or brain infection that I know of. I also don’t recall any single event where my attention or memory suddenly got worse.

F41.1 (anxiety-related condition) is added because anxiety can cause subjective memory and concentration problems and interpersonal stress, but we do not yet have information about worry, tension, or physiological arousal. F32.0 (mood-related condition) is included because depressive episodes frequently manifest with poor concentration, low motivation, and forgetfulness affecting work and home life; we have not yet assessed mood, sleep, appetite, or anhedonia. F07.8 (other organic or cognitive issues) is kept on the early differential because cognitive complaints can be secondary to medical, neurological, or substance-related causes, and we have no medical or substance history yet. At this stage the list is broad and will be refined as more information is gathered.

1) When did these concentration and forgetfulness problems first start? Were you like this as a child in school (e.g., forgetful with homework, easily distracted, often not finishing tasks), or is this more recent?
2) How are you functioning at work or school now—are there performance problems, missed deadlines, or feedback from supervisors/teachers about inattention or disorganization?
3) Do you also struggle with restlessness, acting before thinking, interrupting others, or difficulty waiting your turn, or is it mostly about losing focus and forgetting things?
4) Have you ever had a significant head injury, neurological illness, or major medical condition, or started any new medications or substances (including alcohol, cannabis, or others) around the time these problems began?
5) Over the past six months, how often do you feel worried or tense on a typical day, and does this worry interfere with sleep, concentration, or enjoyment of activities beyond the forgetfulness itself?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports lifelong patterns of inattention beginning in childhood (daydreaming, not finishing chores, talking out of turn) with current difficulties sustaining attention, completing tasks, and forgetfulness that cause functional problems at home and in volunteer work. There is no history of a precipitating neurological event. Anxiety symptoms are present only secondarily (worry about letting people down) and are not pervasive, excessive, or the primary complaint, making generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1) less likely as the main diagnosis.
